title: The bare-minimum ADHD cleaning day (for when it's all too much)
description: A bare minimum ADHD cleaning routine for when everything is too much: three anchor moments, ten minutes total, no deep clean. Enough to hold the line.
h1: When everything is too much, what does a bare-minimum cleaning day actually look like?
target_query: bare minimum cleaning routine for ADHD when everything is too much

faq.q: What is the bare minimum I should clean each day with ADHD?
faq.a: Three anchor moments: a two-minute kitchen close after your last meal, a one-minute bathroom wipe after you brush your teeth, and a three-minute bedroom path clear before bed. That is under ten minutes and it keeps the house livable. Nothing else is required on a bare-minimum day.

faq.q: How long can I run on bare minimum before it becomes a problem?
faq.a: Indefinitely, if the three anchors actually happen. A house on bare minimum is not clean but it is not getting worse, and that is the whole job during a hard stretch. When the stretch ends, one 15-minute reset brings it back. You do not need a deep clean to recover.

faq.q: Why can't I just do a little bit of everything?
faq.a: Because a little bit of everything means deciding what a little bit is, in every room, every day. Decisions are the expensive part for an ADHD brain, especially during a bad stretch. Fixed anchors attached to things you already do remove the deciding, which is why they survive weeks that free-form tidying does not.

sources.supports: Barkley's model frames ADHD as a self-regulation difference where external cues and structure substitute for internal control, which is why anchoring tasks to existing habits works.
Planning and sustained effort on unrewarding tasks are reliably impaired in ADHD, so open-ended daily tidying fails during hard stretches.
Reduced dopamine reward signalling in adult ADHD helps explain why maintenance tasks with no visible payoff are hardest to sustain.
